```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load}
source("R/00_config.R")
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

factors <- read.csv(SCALING_FACTORS)
monthly <- read.csv(MONTHLY_MEANS)
annual <- read.csv(ANNUAL_MEANS)
pairs <- read.csv("output/window_year_pairs.csv")
sensitivity <- read.csv("output/sensitivity.csv")
estimators <- read.csv("output/estimator_comparison.csv")
residuals_df <- read.csv("output/residuals.csv")
diagnostics <- read.csv("output/residual_diagnostics.csv")

pooled <- factors |> filter(site == "pooled", target == "calendar")
prep <- read.csv("output/prep_summary.csv")
label_metric <- function(x) unname(METRIC_LABELS[x])
metric_order <- function(x) match(label_metric(x), unname(METRIC_LABELS))

# Mean leave-one-out error of each estimator, and which pollutants each wins
est_mean <- estimators |>
  group_by(metric, estimator) |>
  summarise(loo = mean(loo_pct_mae), .groups = "drop")

est_best <- est_mean |>
  group_by(metric) |>
  slice_min(loo, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

wins <- function(name) {
  m <- est_best$metric[est_best$estimator == name]
  if (length(m) == 0) "none" else paste(label_metric(m), collapse = " and ")
}

beats_origin <- function(name) {
  cmp <- est_mean |>
    filter(estimator %in% c(name, "through-origin OLS")) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = estimator, values_from = loo)
  m <- cmp$metric[cmp[[name]] < cmp[["through-origin OLS"]]]
  if (length(m) == 0) "no pollutant" else paste(label_metric(m), collapse = " and ")
}
```

# Scope

This document sets out the method behind the scaling factors published in
*Scaling short-term air quality measurements to annual means* and the checks
run against them. The main report states the results and how to use them; this
one states how they were produced, what was assumed, and what happens to the
answers when the assumptions are varied. It is written to be read alongside the
code, which is the definitive statement of the method: every number in both
documents is computed at knit time from the files in `output/`, which are in
turn produced by the scripts named in section [Reproducibility](#reproducibility).

# Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $s$ | A monitoring site, including the synthetic network average |
| $p$ | A pollutant: PM2.5, PM10 or NO2 |
| $y$ | A calendar year |
| $m$ | A calendar month, $1 \dots 12$ |
| $h_{spym}$ | The set of valid hourly measurements in month $m$ |
| $M_{spym}$ | Monthly mean concentration |
| $c_{spym}$ | Completeness of the month: measured hours divided by possible hours |
| $W$ | A sampling window — a run of $n$ consecutive months |
| $X$ | The sampled mean: the mean of the monthly means in $W$ |
| $T$ | The target mean: a calendar-year or rolling twelve-month mean |
| $f$ | The scaling factor, $T \approx f X$ |

# Data preparation

## Source

Hourly measurements are taken from `data/aq_data_SOE2025.RData`, the compiled
dataset behind *Ambient Air Quality in Auckland - trend analysis 2015 to 2024*
(TR 2025/26). It holds one long-format table, `all.data.long`, with columns
`Parameter`, `Value`, `date` and `site`. No re-derivation from raw instrument
output is attempted: the analysis inherits the validation and ratification
applied in producing that dataset. Timestamps are New Zealand local time,
including daylight saving.

## Duplicate timestamps

A site and pollutant occasionally has two records for the same hour, where two
instruments ran in parallel. These are averaged so that each hour contributes
once to the monthly mean. This affects
`r format(prep$n_duplicated, big.mark = ",")` records —
`r sprintf("%.2f", prep$n_duplicated / prep$n_hourly_raw * 100)`% of the hourly
records for these pollutants — concentrated
in NO2 at henderson (2011), queen_st (2012, 2016) and penrose (2006), and PM2.5
at pakuranga (2021) and takapuna (2023). The alternative, taking the first
record, was rejected because the ordering of the source table does not encode
which instrument is preferred.

## Aggregation

Concentrations are aggregated in two steps: hours to monthly means, then
monthly means to the target. The annual mean is therefore the unweighted mean
of twelve monthly means, not the mean of all hours in the year:

$$M_{spym} = \frac{1}{|h_{spym}|}\sum_{t \in h_{spym}} v_t \qquad
T^{\text{cal}}_{spy} = \frac{1}{12}\sum_{m=1}^{12} M_{spym}$$

The two differ whenever data capture is uneven across the year: pooling hours
lets a well-reported month pull the annual figure toward its own level, which
in a seasonal signal means toward its own season. Averaging monthly means gives
each month equal weight regardless of how many hours it contributed. Section
[Sensitivity](#sensitivity) shows the choice makes almost no difference to the fitted
factors, because the completeness rules already exclude the cases where it
would.

## Completeness rules

Two thresholds are applied:

- A **month** is usable if at least
  `r sprintf("%.0f", MIN_MONTH_COMPLETENESS * 100)`% of its possible hours were
  measured ($c_{spym} \geq `r MIN_MONTH_COMPLETENESS`$). Possible hours are
  taken as days in month $\times$ 24, ignoring the one-hour daylight saving
  shifts, which is a rounding of at most 0.15% of a month.
- A **year** is usable only if all twelve of its months are usable. There is no
  partial-year target.

```{r completeness-table}
monthly |>
  group_by(Parameter) |>
  summarise(
    `Site-months` = n(),
    `Excluded` = sum(!complete),
    `Excluded (%)` = mean(!complete) * 100,
    `Median completeness` = median(completeness) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(Pollutant = label_metric(Parameter)) |>
  arrange(metric_order(Parameter)) |>
  select(Pollutant, everything(), -Parameter) |>
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Effect of the monthly completeness rule")
```

The `r sprintf("%.0f", MIN_MONTH_COMPLETENESS * 100)`% figure follows the data
capture conventions usual in ambient monitoring rather than being derived from
this dataset. Because it is a judgement, it is varied in section
[Sensitivity](#sensitivity); the factors move by
`r sensitivity |> filter(variant == "completeness 50%") |> pull(pct_factor_shift) |> abs() |> median() |> sprintf(fmt = "%.1f")`%
(median) when it is relaxed to 50% and
`r sensitivity |> filter(variant == "completeness 90%") |> pull(pct_factor_shift) |> abs() |> median() |> sprintf(fmt = "%.1f")`%
when it is tightened to 90%.

The rule is deliberately strict about the *target*: an annual mean built from
ten months is not the quantity a campaign is trying to estimate, and admitting
one would put error into the thing the error is measured against. The price is
paid in sample size, most heavily for PM2.5.

```{r site-years}
annual |>
  filter(site != CITY_SITE) |>
  count(Parameter, name = "site_years") |>
  mutate(
    Pollutant = label_metric(Parameter),
    `Complete site-years` = site_years,
    `Of a possible` = (END_YEAR - START_YEAR + 1) *
      sapply(Parameter, function(p) {
        monthly |> filter(Parameter == p, site != CITY_SITE) |>
          distinct(site) |> nrow()
      })
  ) |>
  mutate(`Retained (%)` = `Complete site-years` / `Of a possible` * 100) |>
  arrange(metric_order(Parameter)) |>
  select(Pollutant, `Complete site-years`, `Of a possible`, `Retained (%)`) |>
  kable(digits = 0, caption = "Site-years surviving the completeness rules")
```

## The network-average series

A synthetic site, `auckland`, is formed as the mean across all sites reporting
each hour, and carried through the analysis as an extra site. It represents the
network average rather than any location, and its composition changes as sites
enter and leave the record, so:

- it is **excluded from the pooled fits**, where it would double-count the sites
  it is made from;
- it is **excluded from the leave-one-site-out test**, for the same reason;
- it is reported as its own row in `output/scaling_factors.csv` for readers who
  want a network-wide figure.

# Targets

## Calendar year

The primary target. The window sits inside the calendar year it is compared
with, which is the year most reporting is expressed in.

## Rolling twelve months

$$T^{\text{roll}}_{sp,y,m} = \frac{1}{12}\sum_{k=0}^{11} M_{sp,(y,m)+k}$$

where $(y,m)+k$ is the month $k$ months after $(y, m)$, crossing into the
following calendar year as needed. All twelve months must be complete. This is
the target for campaigns that cross the end of a year, and it is anchored at the
window's first month, so the campaign sits at the *front* of the period it
estimates.

Two consequences a reader should hold onto:

1. A rolling-target estimate is not a calendar-year figure and must not be
   reported as one.
2. Anchoring at the front is a choice. A target centred on the campaign would
   probably score better for late-year windows, and was not fitted because a
   period beginning six months before the campaign is rarely the quantity a
   study wants. This is the most questionable of the choices documented here.

## Independence of successive targets

Rolling twelve-month periods overlap, which would ordinarily make the fitted
years dependent. They do not here: a factor is fitted for a fixed window, hence
a fixed start month, so the years entering one fit are anchored twelve months
apart and their targets do not share a single month. The same is true of
calendar years by construction. Cross-year dependence is tested directly in
section [Assumptions and diagnostics](#residual-diagnostics).

# Windows

A window is a run of $n$ consecutive months, $n = 1 \dots `r MAX_WINDOW`$.
Against the calendar-year target the run must lie within one year, giving
$\sum_{n=1}^{`r MAX_WINDOW`}(13-n) = `r nrow(distinct(pooled, window))`$
windows. Against the rolling target it may start in any month, giving
$12 \times `r MAX_WINDOW` = `r 12 * MAX_WINDOW`$, of which
`r factors |> filter(site == "pooled", target == "rolling") |> distinct(window, wraps) |> filter(wraps) |> nrow()`
cross the end of a year.

Only consecutive months are considered. A campaign is a continuous deployment,
so a disjoint set of months — sampling February and August but not the months
between — is not something a single campaign can deliver, and admitting such
sets would multiply the search space to the point where the best window would
be selected on noise.

The window mean $X$ is the unweighted mean of the $n$ monthly means, and the
window is dropped for a year if any of its months is incomplete. A campaign
that does not run the full window is not the window that was fitted.

# The estimator

## Definition

For each pollutant, site (or the pool), window and target, the scaling factor
is the through-origin least squares coefficient across years:

$$\hat{f} = \frac{\sum_i X_i T_i}{\sum_i X_i^2}, \qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{se}}(\hat f) =
\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i (T_i - \hat f X_i)^2}{(n-1)\sum_i X_i^2}}$$

with $i$ indexing the years (and, in a pooled fit, the site-years) available
for that combination. Confidence intervals are reported as
$\hat f \pm 1.96\,\widehat{\operatorname{se}}$; section
[Assumptions and diagnostics](#residual-diagnostics) qualifies the normal approximation behind that.

A minimum of `r MIN_YEARS` years is required before a factor is fitted.

## Why a single multiplier

Three properties recommend it:

- **It is what a campaign can apply.** One number, applied to one measured
  mean. A two-parameter form requires the intercept to hold at a location whose
  concentration level may be nothing like the fitting data's.
- **It matches the error structure.** Absolute errors grow with concentration
  (section [Assumptions and diagnostics](#residual-diagnostics)), so a multiplicative correction is the
  natural form; a fixed additive offset is not.
- **It is scale-free.** The factor for a window is a property of the seasonal
  shape, not of the level, which is what makes it transportable to a site with
  a different mean concentration.

## Alternatives considered {#estimators}

Four estimators were fitted on identical data and scored by the same
leave-one-out procedure.

```{r estimator-table}
est_mean |>
  arrange(metric_order(metric)) |>
  mutate(Pollutant = label_metric(metric)) |>
  select(Pollutant, estimator, loo) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = estimator, values_from = loo) |>
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    caption = "Mean leave-one-out error (%) over all windows, by estimator"
  )
```

```{r estimator-wins}
estimators |>
  group_by(metric, window) |>
  slice_min(loo_pct_mae, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  count(metric, estimator) |>
  mutate(Pollutant = label_metric(metric)) |>
  arrange(metric_order(metric), desc(n)) |>
  select(Pollutant, Estimator = estimator, `Windows won` = n) |>
  kable(caption = "Which estimator scores best, window by window")
```

The definitions, with $r_i = T_i / X_i$:

| Estimator | Formula | Note |
|-----------|---------|------|
| Through-origin OLS | $\sum X_i T_i / \sum X_i^2$ | The published `factor`. Minimises squared *absolute* error, so high-concentration years dominate |
| Ratio of means | $\sum T_i / \sum X_i$ | Same weighting, marginally different fit |
| Mean of ratios | $\frac{1}{n}\sum r_i$ | Every year weighted equally. Published alongside as `ratio_factor` |
| OLS with intercept | $T = a + bX$ | Two parameters, not a scaling factor |

**This comparison does not unambiguously favour the published estimator, and
that should be stated plainly.** Judged on mean leave-one-out percentage error,
the two-parameter model is the best of the four for `r wins("OLS with intercept")`,
and mean-of-ratios beats through-origin OLS for `r beats_origin("mean of ratios")`.
The reason is visible in the weighting column: through-origin OLS minimises
absolute error while the score is a percentage, so it is not the estimator that
optimises the quantity being reported.

The differences are modest — between the three single-factor estimators the
factor itself differs by a median of
`r estimators |> filter(!is.na(factor)) |> group_by(metric, window) |> summarise(d = max(factor) - min(factor), .groups = "drop") |> pull(d) |> median() |> sprintf(fmt = "%.3f")`
— and the through-origin factor is published as the headline for the three
properties in the previous section. But a user optimising for percentage
accuracy at a known site should prefer `ratio_factor`, and one with a long local
record and a concentration level close to the fitting data may do better still
with the two-parameter fit. All three are in `output/scaling_factors.csv`.

# Validation

## Why the fitted error is not quoted

The residuals of a fitted model understate the error on data the model has not
seen, the more so the fewer years are in the fit. Across the pooled fits the
fitted percentage error averages
`r sprintf("%.1f", mean(pooled$pct_mae))`% against
`r sprintf("%.1f", mean(pooled$loo_pct_mae))`% leave-one-out, an understatement
of `r sprintf("%.0f", (1 - mean(pooled$pct_mae) / mean(pooled$loo_pct_mae)) * 100)`%.
Only out-of-sample figures are quoted in the main report.

## Leave-one-out across years

Each year in turn is held out, the factor refitted on the rest, and the held-out
year predicted. For the through-origin estimator this has a closed form, so no
refitting loop is needed:

$$\hat f_{(-k)} = \frac{\sum_i X_i T_i - X_k T_k}{\sum_i X_i^2 - X_k^2},
\qquad e_k = T_k - \hat f_{(-k)} X_k$$

and for the two-parameter model the leave-one-out residuals come from the hat
values, $e_{(-k)} = e_k / (1 - h_k)$.

## Leave-one-site-out

The relevant test for a factor used somewhere it was not fitted. Each site is
removed from the pool entirely, the pooled factor refitted on the remaining
sites, and every year of the held-out site predicted from it. Reported as
`loso_pct_mae` (mean) and `loso_pct_max` (worst single site-year).

## Error metrics

With $e_i$ the relevant residual and $n$ the number of site-years:

| Metric | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| `rmse`, `loo_rmse` | $\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum e_i^2}$, in µg/m³ |
| `pct_mae`, `loo_pct_mae`, `loso_pct_mae` | $\frac{100}{n}\sum |e_i| / T_i$ |
| `loo_pct_max`, `loso_pct_max` | $100 \max_i |e_i| / T_i$ |
| `lm_r_squared` | Coefficient of determination of the two-parameter fit |

Percentage errors are taken relative to the target, not the estimate, so they
answer "how far from the true annual mean is this estimate" rather than the
reverse.

# Uncertainty for a new campaign

A campaign measures $X$ once and reports $\hat T = \hat f X$. Two sources of
error contribute:

1. Uncertainty in the factor itself, $\operatorname{se}(\hat f) \cdot X$. This
   is small — the confidence intervals in the main report span a few per cent —
   and shrinks as the fitting record grows.
2. The year-to-year scatter around the factor, which does not shrink: a given
   year simply may not follow the average seasonal shape.

The second dominates, and it is what `loo_pct_mae` and `loso_pct_mae` measure.
The recommended interval for a campaign estimate is therefore empirical rather
than analytic: take the leave-one-out (own site) or leave-one-site-out (new
site) percentage error for that window and read

$$\hat T \pm \text{loo\_pct\_mae} \times \hat T / 100$$

as a typical band, and `loo_pct_max` as the worst case seen in the record. The
residuals are not normal enough (section [Assumptions and diagnostics](#residual-diagnostics)) to make a
$\pm 1.96\sigma$ interval trustworthy in the tails, and quoting the factor's own
confidence interval alone would understate the true uncertainty by an order of
magnitude.

# Assumptions and diagnostics {#residual-diagnostics}

The method assumes: the seasonal shape at a site is stable across years; the
relationship between window mean and annual mean passes through the origin;
residuals are of roughly constant *relative* size; and successive years are
independent. Each is tested below on the pooled calendar-target fits.

```{r diagnostics-table}
diagnostics |>
  group_by(metric) |>
  summarise(
    `Windows` = n(),
    `cor(|resid|, level)` = median(scale_corr),
    `cor(|rel resid|, level)` = median(rel_scale_corr),
    `Mean rel. residual (%)` = median(mean_rel),
    `Skewness` = median(skewness),
    `Non-normal (% of windows)` = mean(shapiro_p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    `Within-site lag-1` = median(mean_lag1, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(Pollutant = label_metric(metric)) |>
  arrange(metric_order(metric)) |>
  select(Pollutant, everything(), -metric) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Residual diagnostics, median across windows")
```

**Constant relative error — supported.** Absolute residuals grow with
concentration for NO2 (Spearman
`r sprintf("%.2f", diagnostics |> filter(metric == "no2") |> pull(scale_corr) |> median())`),
which is exactly the case an additive correction handles badly. Expressed
relative to the level, that correlation disappears or turns slightly negative in
every pollutant. This is the central justification for a multiplicative factor.

**Independence across years — supported.** Within-site lag-1 autocorrelation of
the residuals is near zero or negative in all three pollutants, so there is no
sign that a site's error in one year carries into the next. The leave-one-out
scores are not inflated by dependence.

**Normality — not supported, and it matters.** Residuals from the pooled fits
fail a Shapiro-Wilk test in
`r sprintf("%.0f", diagnostics |> filter(metric == "no2") |> summarise(x = mean(shapiro_p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) * 100) |> pull(x))`%
of NO2 windows, with positive skew. Pooled fits mix sites of different
character, so this is expected rather than alarming, but it means the
$\pm 1.96\,\operatorname{se}$ confidence intervals on the factors are
approximate, and it is why section 8 recommends empirical error bands rather
than normal-theory prediction intervals.

**Zero intercept — approximately true, and the residual bias is reported.** The
mean relative residual is
`r sprintf("%.1f", median(abs(diagnostics$mean_rel)))`% or less in every
pollutant. It is not exactly zero because through-origin OLS sets the *absolute*
residuals to be orthogonal to $X$, not the relative ones — the same asymmetry
that shows up in the estimator comparison.

**Stable seasonal shape — the weakest assumption.** Section
[Sensitivity](#sensitivity) shows factors fitted on the two halves of the record differ
by a median of
`r sensitivity |> filter(grepl("^period 20(15-2019|20-2024)$", variant)) |> pull(pct_factor_shift) |> abs() |> median() |> sprintf(fmt = "%.1f")`%,
with individual windows moving several times that. The factors describe the
decade averaged, and a campaign in an unusual year is not protected by them.

# Sensitivity {#sensitivity}

Every judgement in the method was varied and the pooled factors refitted from
the raw data. The table reports how far the factors move, as a percentage of
the published value.

```{r sensitivity-table}
sensitivity |>
  filter(variant != "base") |>
  group_by(variant) |>
  summarise(
    `Windows` = n(),
    `Median shift (%)` = median(abs(pct_factor_shift)),
    `90th percentile (%)` = quantile(abs(pct_factor_shift), 0.9),
    `Largest shift (%)` = max(abs(pct_factor_shift)),
    `Median error change (pp)` = median(loo_shift, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  rename(Variant = variant) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Sensitivity of the pooled factors to the method's choices")
```

Reading the table:

- **Completeness threshold.** Relaxing to 50% or tightening to 90% moves the
  factors by under 2% at the median. The rule is not doing hidden work.
- **Annual mean definition.** Weighting months by hours measured, instead of
  equally, changes the factors by
  `r sensitivity |> filter(variant == "hour-weighted annual mean") |> pull(pct_factor_shift) |> abs() |> median() |> sprintf(fmt = "%.2f")`%
  at the median. The completeness rules leave too little uneven capture for the
  choice to matter.
- **Period.** Extending back to `r 2006` or splitting the decade in half moves
  factors by 1.6-2.3% at the median and up to
  `r sensitivity |> filter(grepl("^period", variant)) |> pull(pct_factor_shift) |> abs() |> max() |> sprintf(fmt = "%.0f")`%
  for individual windows. This is the largest sensitivity in the analysis and
  the honest limit on the factors' shelf life: they should be refitted when the
  record extends materially.

```{r rank-stability}
# sensitivity.csv already carries the reference fit as base_factor/base_loo
rank_stability <- sensitivity |>
  filter(variant != "base") |>
  group_by(variant, metric) |>
  summarise(rho = cor(loo_pct_mae, base_loo, method = "spearman"), .groups = "drop")

best_four <- sensitivity |>
  filter(n_months == 4) |>
  group_by(metric, variant) |>
  slice_min(loo_pct_mae, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(metric) |>
  summarise(windows = paste(sort(unique(window)), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")
```

**How stable is the ranking?** The ordering of windows by error is largely
preserved: the Spearman correlation with the published ordering runs from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(rank_stability$rho))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(rank_stability$rho))`
(median `r sprintf("%.2f", median(rank_stability$rho))`), the low end being the
five-year subperiods, which have half the data.

The *single best* window is not equally stable, and the difference is
instructive:

```{r best-window-stability}
best_four |>
  mutate(Pollutant = label_metric(metric)) |>
  arrange(metric_order(metric)) |>
  select(Pollutant, `Best four-month window across all variants` = windows) |>
  kable(caption = "Windows that come top under at least one variant")
```

For NO2 the recommendation survives every variant of the method except the
five-year subperiods, which prefer the neighbouring Jun-Sep. For PM2.5 the top
four-month window moves between Mar-Jun, Aug-Nov and Jul-Oct depending on the
variant — but Mar-Jun and Aug-Nov differ by
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(diff(sensitivity |> filter(variant == "base", metric == "pm2.5", window %in% c("Mar-Jun", "Aug-Nov")) |> pull(loo_pct_mae))))`
percentage points in the published fit, so the two are not meaningfully
separable on this record and the choice between them should not be read as a
finding. This is the thin PM2.5 record showing through, and it is the reason the
main report presents a table of windows rather than a single recommendation.

# Limitations

- **PM2.5 is thinly supported.**
  `r annual |> filter(Parameter == "pm2.5", site != CITY_SITE) |> nrow()`
  complete site-years across
  `r annual |> filter(Parameter == "pm2.5", site != CITY_SITE) |> distinct(site) |> nrow()`
  sites, only
  `r factors |> filter(metric == "pm2.5", site != "pooled", site != CITY_SITE) |> distinct(site) |> nrow()`
  of which has enough years for a site-specific factor.
- **The published estimator is not the best-scoring one** (section
  [Alternatives considered](#estimators)). It is the most portable; the alternatives are supplied.
- **The rolling target is anchored at the campaign start**, not centred on it.
- **Site type is not modelled.** Sites are pooled without a covariate for
  kerbside, urban or rural character, even though the main report shows that
  character drives the residual spread. A mixed model with a site-type term
  would very likely tighten the transfer error; it is the obvious next step and
  was not attempted here.
- **These are Auckland factors**, encoding Auckland's seasonal cycle, emission
  mix and climate.
- **No measurement-uncertainty term.** The analysis treats the reported hourly
  concentrations as exact.
- **Reference-grade instruments only.** Applying a factor to a campaign run on
  a different measurement method assumes that method has already been corrected
  for its own bias.

# Reproducibility {#reproducibility}

```
Rscript R/01_prepare_data.R      # monthly, annual and rolling means
Rscript R/02_scaling_factors.R   # fit the factors
Rscript R/03_figures.R           # report figures
Rscript R/04_method_checks.R     # sensitivity, estimators, residuals (minutes)
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("docs/scaling_factors_report.Rmd")'
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("docs/scaling_factors_methods.Rmd")'
```

Every parameter of the method is in `R/00_config.R`: pollutants, period,
longest window, completeness threshold, minimum years. The data preparation
rules are functions in `R/functions.R` taking those thresholds as arguments, so
that `04_method_checks.R` re-runs the identical code under different settings
rather than a reimplementation of it.

```{r session}
si <- sessionInfo()
pkgs <- c("dplyr", "lubridate", "purrr", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown")
data.frame(
  Package = pkgs,
  Version = sapply(pkgs, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)))
) |>
  rbind(data.frame(Package = "R", Version = paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."))) |>
  kable(row.names = FALSE, caption = paste("Environment:", si$running))
```
